"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The U.S. military has returned all of its long-range bombers stationed at a British
airbase back to the U.S.
As NPR's Greg Myrie reports, this comes just a week after British authorities arrested
and briefly detained five men with suspected ties to Iran near the base.
The U.S. military says all the bombers at Britain's Fairford Air Base in the southwest
part of the country have returned to their home bases.
Vice President J.D. Vance said the move was made out of an abundance of caution.
He also referred to Iranian acts of terrorism against U.S. targets in the past, but did
not offer details on any new threats.
The U.S. has used the base to carry out airstrikes in the war against Iran.
Just over a week ago, British police arrested five young men near the base, raising suspicions
the facility might be a target.
However, the five have all been released on bail.
Greg Myrie, NPR News, Washington.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is throwing its support behind six additional
candidates ahead of the November midterm elections, as NPR's Tamara Keith reports the six candidates
are running in districts where Republicans have an edge.
The committee's red to blue is its top-tier backing for candidates and comes with staff
resources and fundraising support.
All six candidates newly added to the list face challenging races.
Only one is in a district rated by the Cook Political Report as lean Republican.
The others face even longer odds.
For instance, Nevada's second congressional district, where candidate Teresa Benitez Thompson
earned the red to blue nod.
That district has not elected a Democrat since its creation in the early 1980s, a spokesman
for the National Republican Congressional Committee said describing that race as competitive
is delusional.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
One American and two German scientists today were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology
for Medicine, and PR's Rob Stein reports that's for their fundamental discoveries that help
explain how the brain works.
The Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden awarded the prize to two German scientists,
Peter Hegeman and Gerd Nagel, and one American, Karl Deisserhof, at Stanford University.
The three scientists played key roles in discoveries that led to light-controlled switches that
turned nerve cells on and off.
The technique opened a new way to understand the function of neurons known as optogenetics.
The Nobel Committee says the discoveries laid the foundation for a new era of neuroscience,
including helping to understand how the brain forms memories, feelings, and behaviors.
Rob Stein, NPR News.
The U.S. stocks rose near their records today.
The S&P 500 added more than half a percent near its all-high time set over the summer.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Pennsylvania now has more than 1,000 measles cases this year, making it the largest state
outbreak in decades.
Since the beginning of last year, large outbreaks have been reported in several states.
Health experts attribute such outbreaks to low vaccination rates.
The lawyers of six detained journalists in Egypt say the men say they have been subjected
to abuse and forced confessions.
The journalists are facing charges of ties to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, and PR's
Aya Batraoui reports.
Lawyers from the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights say some of the detained men testified
on Sunday before a special branch of the public prosecutor responsible for state security
crimes.
The lawyers say some of the detained men say they were blindfolded, stripped, electrically
shocked, and threatened with harm to their families.
The lawyers say some were also forced to record on-camera fabricated confessions.
The six Egyptian journalists were arrested last week in all work for the fact-checking
independent news website called Metsa Desh, which means don't believe.
The website says it has no affiliation to any political group.
Egypt's Interior Ministry had no immediate comment on the allegations of torture, but
alleged last week the website has ties to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood group and disseminated
false news.
Aya Batraoui, NPR News, Dubai.
Writing advocacy group Penn America says there were nearly 12,000 book bands in public schools
over the past year, the highest since tracking began five years ago.
Stephen King remains the most banned author for the second year.
Many bands occur in Florida and Texas, where restrictive laws and political pressure have
increased removals.
School administrators increasingly use AI to decide which books to ban.
